summary: Task 2 SDK core meets the OWASP focus areas. Ed25519 signing is exclusively via WASM (sign_challenge/sign_cose_payload) — no homemade crypto, no crypto.subtle.sign Ed25519 path, and no @noble/ed25519 import in src/. The /api/sign-callback POST never carries an Authorization header (asserted in client.test.ts:280). All HTTP bodies use JSON.stringify; tag arrays/content/correlation_id are properly serialized/encoded — no string concatenation. Error messages run through redactJWT before throw; redactJWT covers the JWT header+payload segments (both eyJ-prefixed) plus 128-hex Ed25519 secret. New devDependencies (@noble/ed25519@^2.3.0, @noble/hashes@^2.2.0) are scoped to test/ only, are paulmillr's audited libs, contain no postinstall scripts (verified), and exact versions are pinned via bun.lock + package-lock.json. Three low-severity hardening notes recorded below — none block approval.

findings.issue: redactJWT regex /eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}/g does not redact the third (signature) segment of a JWT in isolation. Standard 3-segment JWTs have header+payload both base64url-encoded JSON starting with eyJ, so both are redacted (test client.test.ts:430-451 confirms). However, if only the signature segment leaks into an error string (e.g. a server message like 'invalid signature: SflKxw...'), the regex will not match it because base64url signatures rarely start with eyJ. Practical impact is low: an Ed25519 signature alone is not a forgery primitive and contains no payload claims.
findings.recommendation: Consider augmenting redaction with a JWT-shape pattern that catches the full three-segment form, e.g. /eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]+/g, before falling back to the per-segment regex. Or add an explicit base64url-blob ≥40-char regex when the SDK knows the surrounding context is an auth error.

findings.issue: readBodySafely (client.ts:444-451) truncates the response body to 500 chars BEFORE running redactJWT. If a JWT straddles position 500, the suffix beyond the cutoff is silently dropped (fine) but the prefix that remains may be <20 base64url chars after 'eyJ' and thus skip the redaction. Real JWT headers are ~36 chars so the regex's {20,} threshold typically still matches; the edge case is exotic.
findings.recommendation: Reverse the order: redact first, truncate second. `return redactJWT(txt).slice(0, 500);` — same memory cost, eliminates the slice-then-redact gap entirely.

findings.issue: MnemonicClient.keypairJson holds the in-memory secret (64 bytes including the 32-byte Ed25519 seed) as a plain JS array for the lifetime of the client instance after setKeypair(). There is no zeroize/dispose surface (the signer.ts JSDoc explicitly acknowledges this — see signer.ts:32-34). Defense-in-depth concern only: V8 garbage collection is non-deterministic and JS lacks deterministic destructors. Already partially mitigated by the keypair.toJSON() defensive copy on line 90 (an attacker mutating the original Keypair object cannot tamper with the in-flight signer state).
findings.recommendation: Track in backlog as a Phase 2 concern: a TurnkeySigner / WebAuthnSigner removes the secret from JS heap entirely. For Phase 1 (LocalSigner) the threat model accepts heap exposure — document this explicitly in packages/sdk/README.md when it is added in Task 9.
